name: Prize crossword No 29,583
preamble: For 12 clues an antonym of the solution – of the same length – is to be entered.

clue.text: So, not the right time to diet

blocks.note: first meaning: a clock that is ahead shows the wrong time
second meaning: to go without food

explanation.surface: Someone decides this is a bad moment to start slimming.
explanation.walkthrough: Both meanings lead to FAST: a clock running ahead, and going without food. The preamble says to enter the antonym, so the grid takes SLOW.
explanation.definitionFit: A clock gaining minutes is said to run fast, and abstaining from food is fasting; the opposite of that speed word goes in.

clue.text: Facing surgery, postie gets transferred

indicators.note: things transferred are moved about, so the letters are shifted into a new order

blocks.note: OP is short for an operation
taken as written; a postie is a British postman

explanation.surface: A postman facing an operation finds he has been moved to another round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Facing' looks like part of the story about surgery, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Two houses that face each other across a street stand on contrary sides, which is the preposition's sense.

clue.text: Land up with agent at university

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a rep is a sales representative, an agent for a firm
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Someone ends up hiring a representative while at college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Land up' reads as the phrase meaning to end up; split it, and 'Land' is the definition while 'up' turns the agent around.
explanation.definitionFit: A land is a country or nation, and this South American republic is one example.

clue.text: Old writer’s plot for Office Type

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective describing a type of office

blocks.note: O is the usual abbreviation for old
a pen is a writing implement
a plot is a scheme or plan

explanation.surface: An old author's storyline for a work titled Office Type.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make 'Office Type' look like a book title the old writer is plotting; it is the definition. The 's after writer just joins writer to plot.
explanation.definitionFit: Workplaces with no partition walls, where everyone shares one large floor, are a common layout of modern offices.

clue.text: Good grass is free

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
to grass is British slang for informing on someone, as is to rat
taken as written

explanation.surface: It sounds like a happy announcement that some fine lawn or cannabis costs nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' reads as a noun, but here it is the verb: in British slang to grass is to inform to the police.
explanation.definitionFit: Something given without charge costs nothing, the Latin-derived word for no payment required.

clue.text: Broadcast back-up Miles almost wrecked

indicators.note: almost all of something means it falls just short, so its final letter goes
something wrecked is smashed up, so the letters are broken and rebuilt in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, without the hyphen
the word with its final S removed

explanation.surface: A news report that the backup for someone called Miles has been destroyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' looks like a verb about a news report, and it is the definition, but the rest is not news: it is letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To broadcast information is to spread it widely so that everyone gets to know it.

clue.text: Mighty T. Rex’s taken in air

indicators.note: something taken in is received inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: an air is a tune or song
the initials T and R from the dinosaur's name

explanation.surface: A mighty tyrannosaurus has been lifted up into the air.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds STRONG, which 'Mighty' defines; the preamble says to enter its antonym, so the grid takes FEEBLE. The 's after T. Rex stands for 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mighty and powerful both describe great force; the entered word is its opposite, lacking strength.

clue.text: Predicament of upset weak people

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, and in a down clue that turns the letters upside down

blocks.note: wets is British slang for feeble, ineffectual people

explanation.surface: Weak people get into trouble when they are upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like an adjective about the weak people's feelings, but it is the turnaround signal. Wets are drips or wimps in British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in a stew is an idiom for being in a worried, troubled state or awkward fix.

clue.text: Mistake, extending legs by quarter

blocks.note: legs of a race are laps
a quarter is a compass point, here East

explanation.surface: Someone errs by making the race legs a quarter longer.
explanation.walkthrough: A quarter in crosswords is one of the four compass points: N, S, E or W.
explanation.definitionFit: A lapse is a slip or small error, such as a moment of forgetfulness.

clue.text: Short-term attempt to trap English politician, ‘love god’

indicators.note: to trap something is to catch and hold it, so one piece closes around the others

blocks.note: an attempt is a try
E is the abbreviation for English
a Member of Parliament
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O
Ra is the Egyptian sun god

explanation.surface: A brief bid to snare an English politician styled as a love god.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds TEMPORARY, which 'Short-term' defines; the preamble says to enter its antonym, PERMANENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lasting only a short while is temporary; the entered word is its opposite, lasting indefinitely.

clue.text: Hindu town represented in novel form

indicators.note: to represent something is to present it again in a fresh form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Indian town is portrayed in a work of fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like another rearrangement signal, but it belongs to the definition, 'novel form'.
explanation.definitionFit: A detective story built around a murder mystery is a well-known genre of fiction.

clue.text: Bender makes you totter back, losing key

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters are read from right to left
to lose something is to be left without it, so that letter drops out

blocks.note: to totter is to wobble
B is a musical key

explanation.surface: A drinking binge leaves you staggering backwards and without your door key.
explanation.walkthrough: A bender is British slang for a drinking spree, which the surface uses; here it means something that bends. Turned round, the totter word has a double B, and one goes.
explanation.definitionFit: The joint in the middle of your arm is where it bends, so it is a thing that bends.

clue.text: South-eastern city with American grave

blocks.note: the compass abbreviation for south-east
Rio de Janeiro, the Brazilian city
US for United States, hence American

explanation.surface: A city in the south-east of some country contains an American's burial place.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds SERIOUS, which 'grave' defines; the preamble says to enter its antonym, TRIVIAL. 'Grave' reads as a burial place but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Grave as an adjective means solemn and weighty; the entered word is its opposite, of little importance.

clue.text: Capital university: ‘grabbing balls is immoral!’

indicators.note: to grab something is to clutch it, so one piece holds the other inside

blocks.note: the London School of Economics, a university in the capital
two balls, round like the letter O

explanation.surface: A university in the capital issues a stern warning against groping.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds LOOSE, which 'immoral' defines in its old sense of a loose woman or loose living; the preamble says to enter the antonym, TIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose living means dissolute, immoral conduct; the entered word is the opposite of loose.

clue.text: Hybridize insects or bats without resistance

indicators.note: bats is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild and land in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: Breeding insects or bats with each other meets no opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like it takes the R away, but it is used in its old sense of outside, so R stands with the rest of the letters to be mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: To interbreed two varieties or species is to produce a hybrid, which is crossing them.

clue.text: Apprentice gives boss endless fun

indicators.note: without an end means cut short, so the word loses its tail

blocks.note: a boss is a raised knob or stud
short for entertainment, which is fun

explanation.surface: A trainee gives the boss no end of amusement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' reads as an employer but is the ornamental knob on a shield or ceiling. Entertainment is cut down to its first three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An apprentice is a learner of a trade, and anyone being taught is a learner too.

clue.text: Trump’s possibly millions short, getting thinner!

indicators.note: possibly signals one possible version, so the letters may come in another order
falling short means something is missing, so a letter is taken out

blocks.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for million; this letter is removed

explanation.surface: Perhaps a well-known businessman is millions down and getting slimmer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thinner' looks like the comparative adjective about weight loss, but it is a noun: a solvent that thins paint.
explanation.definitionFit: Turps is short for turpentine, a solvent used to dilute oil paint, which painters call a thinner.

clue.text: In vogue, star chat show booking?

indicators.note: in means inside, so the letters lie within the words that follow

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the next

explanation.surface: A fashionable celebrity is booked for a television interview programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In vogue' reads as a phrase meaning fashionable; here 'In' alone points inside the words. The question mark marks a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A talk show books celebrities to appear and be interviewed, so each one is a booked visitor.

clue.text: Circle Line – many getting on

blocks.note: a circle is shaped like O
L is the abbreviation for line
D is 500 in Roman numerals, a large number

explanation.surface: Crowds board a train on the Circle Line of the London Underground.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds OLD, which 'getting on' defines; the preamble says to enter the antonym, NEW. The Circle Line is a London Underground route.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting on is an idiom for growing elderly; the entered word is the opposite of aged.

clue.text: Useless types clean bowled, say, by spinner initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: to clean is to wash
in cricket, being bowled is one way of being out
the first letter of spinner, a slow bowler in cricket

explanation.surface: A cricket report: hopeless batsmen are clean bowled by the spin bowler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clean bowled' is a cricket phrase for a ball hitting the stumps, but it splits: 'clean' and 'bowled, say'. The 'say' marks bowled as one example of OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A washout is a failure, and people who are failures are called useless types.

clue.text: Acclaim powerless lift

indicators.note: the suffix -less means without, so the abbreviation for this quantity is dropped

blocks.note: to acclaim is to praise

explanation.surface: Someone cheers a broken lift that has no electricity.
explanation.walkthrough: P is the physics symbol for power. The wordplay builds RAISE, which 'lift' defines; the preamble says to enter the antonym, LOWER.
explanation.definitionFit: To lift something is to hoist it upward; the entered word means to bring it down instead.

clue.text: On which many work, said to be frail, numb

definitions.note: the definition is a descriptive phrase for a plural noun

indicators.note: said means spoken, so what follows is judged by its pronunciation

blocks.note: frail means weak
being numb is being in a daze

explanation.surface: Someone who many depend on is described as frail and numb.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole opening phrase; 'On which' wants to be a link, but it describes the days of the working week.
explanation.definitionFit: Monday to Friday are the usual working days for most employees, as opposed to the weekend.

clue.text: Colour wheel associated with wine

definitions.note: a verb: to colour is to blush

blocks.note: to wheel is to turn
red is a kind of wine

explanation.surface: A painter's colour wheel is linked with wine shades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Colour wheel' reads as an artist's chart, but the words split: 'Colour' is the definition, a verb meaning to blush.
explanation.definitionFit: When someone colours with embarrassment, their face flushes and blushes crimson.

clue.text: Take a type of mushroom during operation

indicators.note: during means in the course of, so one piece falls inside the other

blocks.note: an act is an operation or deed
the cep is an edible mushroom, the porcino

explanation.surface: Someone eats a kind of mushroom in the middle of surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds ACCEPT, which 'Take' defines; the preamble says to enter the antonym, REFUSE.
explanation.definitionFit: To take an offer is to agree to receive it; the entered word means to turn it down.

clue.text: Order child to turn over rubbish

indicators.note: turning something over flips it, so the letters are read the other way

blocks.note: a kid is a child
tat is British slang for cheap, worthless goods

explanation.surface: A parent tells a child to sort through the junk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' looks like the parent's instruction in the story, and it is the definition, but a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A diktat is a harsh decree imposed without consultation, so it is a command.

clue.text: Miss dancing, if a temptation

indicators.note: dancing means moving about, so these letters move into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
a lure is a temptation

explanation.surface: A young lady finds dancing tempting.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds FAILURE, which 'Miss' defines; the preamble says to enter the antonym, SUCCESS. 'Miss' reads as a young woman, but here it is a failed attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: A miss is a shot that fails to hit; the entered word is its opposite, a hit.

clue.text: Slice a few rocks by river

indicators.note: rocks is a verb here, to shake or sway, so the letters are shaken up

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Someone cuts a few stones beside a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocks' looks like a plural noun for stones, but it is a verb meaning shakes.
explanation.definitionFit: A wafer is a very thin piece of something, like a thin slice of ham or silicon.

clue.text: I say Latin is quite acceptable

blocks.note: coo is a British exclamation of surprise, like I say
L is the abbreviation for Latin

explanation.surface: A speaker declares that using Latin is perfectly fine.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds COOL, which 'quite acceptable' defines in its informal sense; the preamble says to enter the antonym, WARM, taking the temperature sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is cool means it is fine or allowed; the entered word is the opposite of cold.

clue.text: Unawareness of topless Italian can possibly lead to embarrassment

indicators.note: with its top removed, a word across loses its first letter
possibly suggests one of several versions, so the letters may be rearranged
the lead of something is its front, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: signor, the Italian for a gentleman, without its first letter
taken as written
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Not knowing about a bare-chested Italian could leave you blushing.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds IGNORANCE, which 'Unawareness' defines; the preamble says to enter the antonym, KNOWLEDGE. Signor is the Italian form of address for a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignorance means lack of awareness or information; the entered word is the opposite, knowing things.

clue.text: Affordable affluent housing sheet

indicators.note: housing means giving shelter, so the words hold the letters inside them

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A report on affordable housing for wealthy people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affordable housing' is a familiar phrase in planning debates, which hides that 'housing' is the signal to look inside the words.
explanation.definitionFit: A leaf of a book or of paper is a single page or thin layer of material.

clue.text: Firm shiver on removing top

indicators.note: in a down clue the top is the first letter, so that letter is taken off

blocks.note: a shiver is a splinter or broken fragment, as is a shard

explanation.surface: A company starts to shake when someone takes off their top.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds HARD, which 'Firm' defines; the preamble says to enter the antonym, EASY. 'Shiver' looks like a verb about cold, but it is a noun meaning a fragment.
explanation.definitionFit: Firm as an adjective means solid or tough; the entered word is the opposite, as in simple.

clue.text: Proof saint’s conversion in balance

indicators.note: a conversion changes something into a different form, so the letters are reworked
in means inside, so the reworked letters sit within the other piece

blocks.note: taken as written; the 's joins it to what follows
the rest is the balance, what remains

explanation.surface: The proof that a saint converted to the faith hangs in the balance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Proof' reads as evidence, but here it is the suffix sense in words like waterproof: able to withstand.
explanation.definitionFit: Something proof against water or fire withstands it, so it holds out against attack.

clue.text: Fool around next to chasm

indicators.note: around means encircling, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: an ass is a fool
by means beside, next to

explanation.surface: Someone clowns about dangerously near the edge of a ravine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fool around' reads as one phrase meaning to mess about; it splits into the fool and the signal to wrap him round the next piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A chasm is a deep, seemingly bottomless gulf in the earth, a deep pit.
